name: Mexoryl SX (ecamsule)

lead: Mexoryl SX (ecamsule) is L'Oreal's UVA filter, used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers by people aiming to limit sun-driven skin aging and pigmentation. Blocking UVA means slower photoaging and a more even tone.

It absorbs UVA with a peak near 345 nm and is described as photostable. It has more human data than most newer filters: a 1998 study reported protection of human skin against repeated UVA doses, and a 2008 review summarised clinical results of Mexoryl SX sunscreens, including UVA-induced skin changes and photoaging markers.

paras: It appears in products such as Anthelios and La Roche-Posay sunscreens and is applied as an everyday step on the face and body. It is one of the few newer UVA filters available in the US.

A 2019 JAMA trial found it detectable in blood after maximal-use application, above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold for further testing; the paper does not conclude this indicates harm. Photoallergy to sunscreens is described as rare.

angle.text: Mexoryl SX is L'Oreal's UVA filter, used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers to limit sun-driven skin aging. Absorbing UVA means slower photoaging and more even tone, and it has human photoprotection and absorption data.

lead: Ecamsule, known commercially as Mexoryl SX (INCI name terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid), is a water-soluble organic UVA filter developed by L'Oreal. It is used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers to protect skin from UVA, the part of sunlight associated with photoaging, pigmentation and wrinkling, so that skin keeps a more even, youthful look.[1]

It absorbs across roughly 290 to 400 nm with a peak near 345 nm, and Wikipedia describes it as intrinsically photostable, unlike avobenzone, which usually needs stabilisers.[1] L'Oreal patented it in 1982, and it was approved in the EU in 1991.[1]

It has been studied more extensively than many newer filters. A 1998 study reported protection of human skin against repeated sub-erythemal UVA doses, a 2008 review summarised clinical results of Mexoryl SX sunscreens, and a 2019 JAMA trial found that ecamsule and three other sunscreen ingredients reached plasma concentrations above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold under maximal-use conditions.[2][3][4]

paras: Ecamsule is a camphor-derived molecule with sulfonic acid groups, usually neutralised so it dissolves in the water phase of formulations.[5] Wikipedia gives its formula as C28H34O8S2 and notes that, as an acid, it is typically neutralised with triethanolamine so it does not shift the product pH too much.[1] It is commonly paired with other filters, including Mexoryl XL (drometrizole trisiloxane), with which it is reported to act synergistically.[5][1]

On exposure to UV the molecule undergoes reversible photoisomerisation, releasing absorbed energy as heat, and Wikipedia reports it as photostable.[1] Because it covers only part of the UV spectrum, it is formulated alongside other filters for broad-spectrum protection.[1]

L'Oreal patented ecamsule in 1982, and it was approved in the EU in 1991, with sunscreens containing it reaching Europe, Canada and other markets from 1993.[1] The US FDA approved it in July 2006, but only for sunscreens registered under a New Drug Application rather than as a freely usable ingredient.[1]

A sunscreen overview on Wikipedia lists ecamsule as permitted in Australia, Canada, the EU, Japan and the US, with a maximum of 10% in most of these and 3% in the US, and notes that the US treats sunscreen filters as over-the-counter drugs while the EU treats them as cosmetics, so fewer filters are available in the US (29 in the EU and 17 in the US as of 2023).[6]

In a 1998 study, volunteers received repeated sub-erythemal UVA exposures over 13 weeks and the authors evaluated whether Mexoryl SX protected against resulting skin changes.[2] A 2008 review summarised clinical studies of Mexoryl SX sunscreens against UV-induced skin effects.[4] A 2000 study of a full-spectrum daily cream reported protection against biological changes involved in photoaging.[7] A 2004 paper examined prevention of UV-induced pigmentation.[8] A photoprovocation study evaluated sunscreens in patients with photosensitive lupus erythematosus.[9]
Wikipedia reports that a 5% ecamsule sunscreen prevented early photoaging changes in humans and that, combined with avobenzone and octocrylene, it reduced UV-related skin damage in human subjects.[1]

A 2003 study compared percutaneous absorption in human volunteers with in vitro data.[10] The 2019 JAMA randomised trial measured blood levels of avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene and ecamsule from four sunscreens; the paper discusses the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold for further toxicology work.[3] A 2010 photopatch study included Anthelios SX, which contains Mexoryl SX, and reported true photoallergy to sunscreens as rare.

Wikipedia describes ecamsule as showing little percutaneous absorption and few systemic effects, notes a mouse study finding no increase in skin cancer promotion, and reports in vitro studies finding it not photomutagenic.[1]

Human studies include a 1998 repeated-UVA exposure study, a 2000 photoaging-cream study, a 2000 lupus photoprovocation study, a 2004 pigmentation study, a 2003 absorption study, the 2019 JAMA absorption trial and a 2008 review.[2][3][4][7][8][9][10]
